comment: Why a SwiftUI symbol is absent from TUIkit, on purpose.
renamed        - the capability exists under a different name. 'tuikit' is that
name, and the tool checks it still exists.
notImplemented - deliberately absent. 'why' must say what a CHARACTER GRID cannot
express, not merely that the API sounds graphical.
differentShape - the capability exists but not as a one-to-one symbol; 'how'
is prose and is NOT machine-checked, so keep it short and true.
families       - glob patterns, for whole families that share one reason.
An entry explains everything inside it: explaining AccessibilityRotor also explains
AccessibilityRotor.Body. Anything neither explained here nor listed in baseline.json
is reported as a gap. Run with --stale to have the tool check these entries back
against both frameworks; an entry that has gone wrong is worse than no entry.

families.why: A terminal has no assistive-technology stack: no VoiceOver, no rotor, no accessibility tree for anything to read. The screen reader IS the terminal's own, driven by the text TUIkit already emits, so contrast and labelling are the levers that carry over — and those are TUIkit's own API.
Xcode canvas metadata. It has no runtime meaning in any app, on any platform.

SwiftUI's gesture algebra composes continuous multi-touch streams. A terminal reports discrete press/release/wheel events with no pressure, no velocity and no simultaneous touches, so there is nothing for a recognizer to arbitrate. TUIkit exposes the events it does get: onTapGesture, onHover, and drag-and-drop.
AttributedString attribute scopes describe font, kerning and paragraph metrics a cell grid does not have. TUIkit styles runs with its own Text attributes.
Standard-library conformance members. They appear on both sides wherever the type does, so comparing them measures Hashable and Collection, not parity.
Every View has one. Where TUIkit implements the view it has a body too, so a difference here only ever means the TYPE is absent — which is reported on the type itself.

TUIkit has `Animatable`, `AnimatablePair`, `AnimatableValues` and `VectorArithmetic`, and interpolates through them. What stays absent under this rule: the conformances on types TUIkit does not have (CoreGraphics geometry, decisions C1; SwiftUI's shapes, O0 of the refusal review; `Color.ResolvedHDR`, A16), the deprecated `AnimatableModifier`, and the `@Animatable`/`@AnimatableIgnored` macros, which need a swift-syntax macro plugin (decisions A52).

The typeface axes: naming a family, asking for a point size, scaling one, or widening it. A terminal emulator draws every cell in the one font at the one size its user configured, and no escape sequence asks it for another — so each of these could only be accepted and ignored. TUIkit's Font (Sources/TUIkit/Styling/Font.swift) carries the axes that DO survive: the semantic style, weight and italic.

Small caps is a glyph variant inside a typeface — real capitals at x-height. A terminal font has one glyph per codepoint and no variant table. `View.textCase(.uppercase)` is not this API under another name: it substitutes different CHARACTERS, changing what the text says and (for ß → SS) how many cells it needs.

SwiftUI can put a searchable field's suggestions in two places — a pop-up menu, or in the content beneath the field — so it needs a placement type and a per-placement visibility. TUIkit has one place: the field's drop-down (Sources/TUIkit/Views/TextInputSuggestions.swift, the same DropdownMenu the Picker uses). `View.searchSuggestions(_:)` and `View.searchCompletion(_:)` are implemented against it. Shipping the `for:` overload would mean either honouring one case of an OptionSet and silently ignoring the other — the partial-seam shape declined twice in Documentation/Parity-decisions-pending.md — or inventing an in-content suggestions surface, which is a feature rather than parity plumbing.

The `image:` spelling of these initializers names an `ImageResource` — a symbol the Xcode build generates from an asset catalogue, whose value is a raster bitmap at one of several scale factors. A terminal app has neither: no asset catalogue in the build (SwiftPM resources are files, not named image constants), and no way to place a bitmap in a cell. The `systemImage:` spelling of every one of these IS implemented (Sources/TUIkit/SFSymbols/ControlSymbolInitializers.swift), because an SF Symbol is a character: it resolves to a Private-Use scalar the terminal font may carry, and falls back to the title alone when it does not. `Label(_:image:)` and `ContentUnavailableView(_:image:description:)` with an image NAME (a String) ship, the name found as `Image(_:bundle:)` finds a resource file (refusal review P12); their `ImageResource` forms share the parity key and stay declined by this rule.

The `formatter:` spelling is the pre-`FormatStyle` class API. It parses through an untyped out-parameter — `Formatter.getObjectValue(_:for:errorDescription:)` yields `AnyObject` — so binding it to a `Binding<Int>` is a downcast the compiler cannot check, and SwiftUI's `Text`/interpolation overloads narrow it further to `NSObject` and `ReferenceConvertible`, which are Objective-C bridging protocols rather than Swift ones. The same capability IS implemented in its typed form, where `Strategy.ParseOutput == FormatInput` makes the round-trip a static guarantee: `TextField(_:value:format:)` and its two siblings (Sources/TUIkit/Views/TextFieldValue.swift), `Text(_:format:)` (Sources/TUIkit/Views/Text.swift:111) and `\(value, format:)` in a LocalizedStringKey interpolation. Adding the class spelling beside them would be the same feature with the type safety taken out.

SwiftUI's hook for writing an animation CURVE of your own, by integrating a value forward from a mutable per-animation state. TUIkit's animations are closed-form functions of elapsed time on purpose, not integrated: that is what lets a repeating one be sampled once and handed to the run loop as finished frames (AnimatedCellRun), which is the whole difference between a decoration costing nothing and costing a render pass twenty times a second. A protocol whose contract is 'you may keep state between frames' cannot offer that, so adopting it would mean two animation models, one of which is never cheap.

Wrapping an AppKit view, view controller, gesture recogniser or app delegate inside SwiftUI. There is no AppKit on a character grid, and TUIkit must also build on Linux, where none of these types exist. The escape hatch a terminal offers instead is `Renderable` — a view that assembles its own cells — not a bridge to a second view system.

Per-pixel shading: Metal shader functions, colour/layer/distortion effects, blur, glass materials, blend modes, luminance to alpha, the background extension effect (a mirrored, blurred copy) and dynamic range. Every one of them addresses a sample. A terminal cell has one foreground colour, one background colour and a glyph, with no subpixel to shade. `View.opacity` is the one filter that survives, and it survives by resolving at composite time against whatever is behind it (see Documentation/Opacity as composition.md) rather than by blending pixels.
visionOS: three-dimensional spatial events, immersive spaces, world tracking, the compositor and RealityKit content. A terminal is a flat grid of cells with no depth, no head pose and no hands.
Apple Pencil hover, squeeze and double-tap. Hardware a terminal cannot see: its input is bytes arriving on a file descriptor.
The Touch Bar — a strip of pixels on a keyboard Apple no longer ships. No terminal has one to draw into.

Windows and the desktop window server: opening, sizing, positioning, restoring, minimising, full-screen and resize behaviour, multiple windows, the menu-bar extra, the Settings scene and an alert that is itself a scene. A TUI app owns exactly one surface — the terminal it was launched in — whose size the user's terminal emulator decides and announces by SIGWINCH. There is nothing for the application to open, place, or dismiss.

The document architecture and the system file panels: DocumentGroup, FileDocument, the importer/exporter/mover sheets and the Services menu. Each presents an AppKit panel backed by file coordination and UTType, and TUIkit has no window to present one in. An app that needs a file picker draws it from `List` and the file system.

The mouse cursor's SHAPE. A terminal emulator owns its own pointer and its own cursor image; an application is told where a click landed and nothing more. No terminal protocol lets an app ask for a resize cursor over a divider.

Writing Tools: Apple's on-device language models, which macOS presents over a text view to proofread, rewrite and summarise. A terminal app has no such service to call. (The in-app find bar this family once also declined ships for TextEditor: findNavigator, findDisabled, replaceDisabled and FindContext, refusal review P17.)

The macOS 26 drag-session API: sessions, containers, formations and multi-item previews, with per-operation policies negotiated between processes. TUIkit's drag and drop lives inside one terminal process — `draggable(_:)`, `dropDestination(for:action:isTargeted:)` and ForEach's row reordering. What this rule excuses is the cross-process session machinery, which would need a pasteboard server and a drag image something has to composite.

The menu-bar command system — CommandMenu, CommandGroup and their placements — plus `onCommand`'s responder-chain selectors. A terminal has no menu bar. SwiftUI-compatibility.md §2.6 records the substitute: TUIkit's chrome is a status bar of shortcut hints built from `StatusBarItem`, whose identity IS the shortcut it announces.
WidgetKit configurations and control widgets. They are built by a separate extension process that the system renders into the Home Screen and Control Centre. A terminal app is not one.
ShareLink and its previews present the system share sheet, which enumerates other applications' share extensions. Outside a windowed OS session there is no such registry to enumerate.

The modifiers, environment values and initialisers over Image.Scale, SymbolRenderingMode, SymbolColorRenderingMode and SymbolVariableValueMode, whose types are declined above. An SF Symbol here is one codepoint drawn at the terminal's font size in the cell's single foreground colour (Sources/TUIkit/SFSymbols/SFSymbol.swift). So there is no relative size to pick (macOS honours imageScale: 17×16 → 23×20 points, measured), no layers to colour separately (macOS draws even single-layer `star` differently under .hierarchical), and no variable-value layers to fill. Confirmed in Documentation/SwiftUI-API-completion-refusal-review.md (Symbols).

Sub-cell typography: kerning and tracking move glyphs by fractions of a point, baselineOffset raises a run within its line, and lineHeight sets the distance between baselines. Cells advance in whole columns and rows, and the emulator places each glyph within its cell, so none of these could be more than accepted and ignored. Confirmed in Documentation/SwiftUI-API-completion-refusal-review.md (P8's omissions, and the Font.Leading verdict: a grid can only move whole rows).

Affordances the operating system draws over a text view: Apple Intelligence's Writing Tools button, and the rich-text formatting control bar. Nothing in a terminal app is OS-drawn, and neither service reaches a terminal. TextInputFormattingControlPlacement is declined for the same reason (Documentation/SwiftUI-API-completion-refusal-review.md).

A run's typesetting language sets its line height, line breaking and spacing. Line height is the terminal's row and spacing is whole cells; TUIkit's word wrapper breaks at spaces and at characters a line cannot hold, whatever the language. So a language changes none of the three and could only be accepted and ignored. See Documentation/SwiftUI-API-completion-decisions.md C8.
visionOS: immersive spaces, Compositor Services content, hand-gesture shortcuts and world recentring. None of these is available on macOS, and a terminal has no space to be immersed in.

WidgetKit controls and system surfaces: Control Center and Lock Screen controls, a widget's invalidatable content, interaction tracking for system intelligence, and iOS Assistive Access's navigation icon. Each is drawn by the system outside the app, and no such surface reaches a terminal app.

AppKit bridges: SwiftUI content hosted in an NSMenu or an NSWindow sheet, scene representations for NSApplication, AppKit animations driven by a SwiftUI Animation, and conversions to AppKit value types. TUIkit draws no AppKit views, and AppKit is absent on Linux and Windows; Renderable is the escape hatch for drawing of an app's own.

Handoff and URL delivery: NSUserActivity continuation, and URLs opened from elsewhere arriving at the app. Both come through the app's bundle registration with LaunchServices, which a command-line program run in a terminal has none of; nothing can send it a URL or an activity.

iOS device and lifecycle features: interface orientation (for previews and supported orientations), background tasks woken by the system, and the home indicator and other persistent system overlays. A terminal app has none of them, on any platform.

Core Data, which is absent on Linux and Windows. Offering it behind #if canImport(CoreData) would be a policy change (no Apple-only public API surface) rather than a medium limit; Documentation/SwiftUI-API-completion-refusal-review.md confirms the same decline for SectionedFetchRequest.
StoreKit's subscription-status view, driven by the App Store. Absent off Apple platforms, and an app run from a terminal is not sold through the App Store.

macOS window and menu-bar chrome: window and menu-bar-extra styles, window placement, utility windows, which scenes launch or are restored, and the shortcut that opens a scene's window. The terminal emulator owns the one window a TUIkit app draws in. Further scenes are the multi-scene question, Documentation/SwiftUI-API-completion-refusal-review.md O9.

Combine: an ObservableObject injected as an environment object, and a Combine publisher's values. Combine is absent on Linux and Windows. TUIkit's observable path is Observation's: inject with .environment(_:) and read with @Environment(Model.self), the mapping EnvironmentObject's differentShape entry records. A publisher becomes an AsyncSequence consumed in .task(id:).

Mesh gradients need per-pixel interpolation, and haptics need hardware a terminal does not have. Spring-loading (activating a control by pausing over it during a drag) was caught by name by the old spring rule; Spring and every spring animation now ship. The Wave 17 review (P11) reopens all three: MeshGradient and SpringLoadingBehavior as implementable, SensoryFeedback as O8.

The animator VIEWS: content described at each phase, or by a keyframe timeline, with the framework moving between them. Pre-rendering a subtree once per phase runs its render side effects once per phase (focus registration, hit-test regions, onAppear, preference writes); the live alternative — each step a withAnimation, rendering every frame while it runs — is O2 of the Wave 17 review, an owner decision. The keyframe timeline itself (KeyframeTimeline, Keyframes, KeyframeTrack, the four keyframes) ships; `View.transition(_:)` and `AnimatedCellRun` cover the cases the views would, from the two ends.

Per-pixel shading: Metal shader functions, colour/layer/distortion effects, glass materials, blend modes and dynamic range. Every one of them addresses a sample. A terminal cell has one foreground colour, one background colour and a glyph, with no subpixel to shade. The colour effects (brightness, contrast, saturation, grayscale, hue rotation) rewrite cell colours and ship, as View modifiers and as visual effects; `View.opacity` is the one filter that survives, and it survives by resolving at composite time against whatever is behind it (see Documentation/Opacity as composition.md) rather than by blending pixels.

Font.Weight.why: Sources/TUIkit/Styling/StyleAttributes.swift:24 — the enum is spelled `FontWeight` at the top level, and `Font.Weight` is a typealias to it (Sources/TUIkit/Styling/Font.swift), so SwiftUI's spelling and every case (`Font.Weight.bold`, `.light`, …) compile verbatim. The audit reads declarations rather than resolving typealiases, so it sees the members only under the top-level name.

GlobalCoordinateSpace.why: `CoordinateSpace.global`, relative to the terminal's top-left cell. One caveat, documented on `GeometryReader`: `.global` is exact only when the renderer knows the reader's on-screen origin, and otherwise falls back to the local frame rather than inventing a position (`hasGlobalPosition` says which).

ImageRenderer.why: Rendering a view off screen into an inspectable result is public: `renderToBuffer(_:context:) -> FrameBuffer`, whose output reads as `FrameBuffer.lines`. There is no image to make: the result is cells.

LocalCoordinateSpace.why: Sources/TUIkit/Views/GeometryReader.swift:99-100 — `case local`, "Relative to the GeometryReader itself, whose origin is (0, 0)", consumed by `frame(in:)` at :49-58 where it is documented as "always exact". SwiftUI's struct is just the protocol-based spelling of the same case.

ProposedViewSize.why: Sources/TUIkitCore/Rendering/LayoutTypes.swift:16 — `public struct ProposedSize` with `width: Int?` / `height: Int?` and `.unspecified` / `.fixed(_:_:)`. Same role and same nil-means-ideal semantics as `ProposedViewSize`, in cells rather than CGFloat per §2.2. It is what `Layout.

ScrollTargetBehavior.why: Sources/TUIkit/Views/ScrollGranularity.swift:22-27. TUIkit answers "where may the viewport rest" with a closed two-case enum (.line / .row) rather than an open protocol an app conforms to; `.row` is the view-aligned rule.

ToolbarContent.why: /Users/robot/Documents/TUIkit/Sources/TUIkit/StatusBar/StatusBarItem.swift:118-130 — the protocol a bar item conforms to (shortcut, label, triggerKey, order, matches(_:)). It is the item-content abstraction the status bar consumes, the role ToolbarContent plays for a toolbar.

ToolbarItem.why: `StatusBarItem(shortcut:label:key:order:displayInStatusBar:action:)`. An item is a shortcut and a label rather than arbitrary `@ViewBuilder` content, because the bar is one line of shortcut hints; toolbars are decisions A28.

ViewAlignedScrollTargetBehavior.why: `ScrollGranularity.row`, applied with `.scrollGranularity(.row)`: the viewport moves a whole row at a time and the top row is always fully visible. The same behaviour, without a `scrollTargetLayout()` marker, because List and Table enumerate their rows; decisions A6 asks whether to adopt SwiftUI's protocol.

AXChartDescriptorRepresentable.why: Conformance requires AXChartDescriptor from Apple's Accessibility framework, which does not exist on Linux — a hard blocker for a package that must build there (.claude/CLAUDE.md) — and its purpose is VoiceOver's audio graph, for which a pty has no channel.

AccessibilityActionCategory.why: It categorises custom AX actions (.default/.edit) inside the AX actions menu, a VoiceOver UI. TUIkit surfaces extra actions as drawn menus instead (Sources/TUIkit/Modifiers/ContextMenuModifier.swift:332), which need no AX category because they are ordinary visible items.

AccessibilityAdjustmentDirection.why: It exists only as the argument of `accessibilityAdjustableAction`'s callback, which an assistive technology invokes, and a terminal app has none to invoke it. The adjustment a person makes arrives as ordinary key input instead: the arrow keys, through `onKeyPress`.

AccessibilityAttachmentModifier.why: It is the opaque ModifiedContent modifier that carries AX attachments up the view tree (the return type of nearly every accessibility* modifier). With no accessibility attachments to carry — TUIkit has none anywhere in Sources — the type has nothing to represent.

AccessibilityChildBehavior.why: It is the parameter of accessibilityElement(children:) (.combine/.contain/.ignore), describing how children fold into an AX element. TUIkit's render produces a flat cell grid with no element tree, so there are no children to fold.

AccessibilityCustomContentKey.why: It keys reader-only supplementary content used with AXCustomContent.Importance, an Apple-only Accessibility-framework type absent on Linux. Content that is never drawn cannot reach a terminal user.

AccessibilityDirectTouchOptions.why: Its options (requiresActivation, silentOnTouch) configure VoiceOver's direct-touch pass-through on a touch screen. A terminal has no digitizer — input is key bytes and cell-granular SGR mouse reports — so there is nothing to configure.

AccessibilityHeadingLevel.why: h1…h6 exist for rotor navigation over an AX tree. TUIkit draws headings (Sources/TUIkit/Views/Section.swift:47) but a level number that is never rendered has no consumer in a terminal, where the only 'reader' sees the finished characters.

AccessibilityLabeledPairRole.why: The .label/.content roles only mean something to accessibilityLabeledPair's AX association. The visible pairing a terminal can express already exists as Sources/TUIkit/Views/LabeledContent.swift:25.

AccessibilityRotorContent.why: It is the content protocol for rotor entry lists, consumed by VoiceOver's rotor. No assistive technology can attach to a process whose interface is a byte stream on a pty.

AccessibilityRotorContentBuilder.why: A result builder that exists purely to construct AccessibilityRotorContent; with no rotor to build for, the builder has nothing to produce.

AccessibilityRotorEntry.why: An entry in a VoiceOver rotor, optionally scoped to a text range. A terminal exposes no navigable element or text-range model to any assistive technology — the emulator's screen buffer is all that exists outside the process.

AccessibilitySystemRotor.why: Its members (.headings, .links, .tables, .misspelledWords…) name VoiceOver's built-in rotors. TUIkit renders links, tables and headings as characters; there is no rotor UI in a terminal to enumerate them into.

AccessibilityTechnologies.why: An option set of .voiceOver and .switchControl used to ask which assistive technology is active. Neither can attach to a TUIkit process: they inspect a GUI app's AX tree, and a TUIkit app has no window — the terminal emulator owns the only inspectable surface.

AccessibilityTextContentType.why: Its cases (.sourceCode, .console, .spreadsheet…) tune a reader's pronunciation and navigation. The classification is never rendered, and nothing in a terminal reads app-side metadata.

AccessibilityTraits.why: The trait option set (isButton, isSelected, isHeader, allowsDirectInteraction, causesPageTurn…) is AX-tree metadata. TUIkit publishes no AX tree; a terminal app conveys role only by what it draws (button caps, selection highlight, Section headers).

AccessibilityZoomGestureAction.why: It describes a VoiceOver pinch/zoom gesture (direction, location, point). SGR mouse reporting has no pinch and no sub-cell location, and there is no assistive technology to originate the gesture. TUIkit's real zoom is `.imageZoom(_:)` at Sources/TUIkit/Views/Image.swift:453.

AnyShape.why: Type erasure over a Shape protocol that does not and cannot exist here (see Shape). TUIkit's erasure story is AnyView / AnyLayout (Sources/TUIkit/Views/AnyLayout.swift) — there is nothing shape-shaped to erase.

AssistiveAccess.why: A Scene that supplies an alternate interface for iOS's Assistive Access mode. A terminal app has no iOS lifecycle and no system mode to supply one for.

BlendMode.why: There is no blend function for it to name. A composite copies each cell over what it covers; the one blend TUIkit performs, `opacity`, resolves at the composite against whatever is behind (Documentation/Opacity as composition.md). The modes multiply, screen and so on per pixel sample, which a cell does not have: see the per-pixel shading family.

ButtonBorderShape.why: Capsule/circle/roundedRectangle radii are vector paths; a cell-grid button can only pick bracket glyphs (Sources/TUIkit/Views/Button.swift:55) or box corner glyphs (BorderStyle.rounded, Sources/TUIkitStyling/Styles/BorderStyle.swift:109). No radius exists to name.

Capsule.why: A capsule is two semicircular end caps; the terminal's cap vocabulary is two half-block characters, TerminalSymbols.openCap (▐) and closeCap (▌) at Sources/TUIkitCore/Rendering/TerminalSymbols.swift:18-21 — a fixed pair of glyphs, not a parameterised curve.

CGPoint.AnimatableData.why: SwiftUI conforms CGPoint/CGSize/CGRect to its Animatable; TUIkit cannot conform them to its own. On Apple platforms SwiftUICore's extension of these CoreGraphics types is visible to any module that imports Foundation (a cross-import overlay), and its `AnimatableData` typealias is found before any witness TUIkit could supply, so the conformance fails to compile there (verified 2026-10-03). TUIkit's geometry is whole cells: `CellSize` and `CellRect` are Animatable (Sources/TUIkit/Rendering/AnimatableGeometry.swift). `CGFloat` IS conformed: Sources/TUIkitCore/Animation/VectorArithmetic.swift.

CGPoint.applying(_:).why: Applies a ProjectionTransform, a 3-D perspective matrix (declined under its own entry): a cell grid has no projection to apply a point through.

CGRect.AnimatableData.why: SwiftUI conforms CGPoint/CGSize/CGRect to its Animatable; TUIkit cannot conform them to its own. On Apple platforms SwiftUICore's extension of these CoreGraphics types is visible to any module that imports Foundation (a cross-import overlay), and its `AnimatableData` typealias is found before any witness TUIkit could supply, so the conformance fails to compile there (verified 2026-10-03). TUIkit's geometry is whole cells: `CellSize` and `CellRect` are Animatable (Sources/TUIkit/Rendering/AnimatableGeometry.swift). `CGFloat` IS conformed: Sources/TUIkitCore/Animation/VectorArithmetic.swift.

CGSize.AnimatableData.why: SwiftUI conforms CGPoint/CGSize/CGRect to its Animatable; TUIkit cannot conform them to its own. On Apple platforms SwiftUICore's extension of these CoreGraphics types is visible to any module that imports Foundation (a cross-import overlay), and its `AnimatableData` typealias is found before any witness TUIkit could supply, so the conformance fails to compile there (verified 2026-10-03). TUIkit's geometry is whole cells: `CellSize` and `CellRect` are Animatable (Sources/TUIkit/Rendering/AnimatableGeometry.swift). `CGFloat` IS conformed: Sources/TUIkitCore/Animation/VectorArithmetic.swift.

Circle.why: A curve needs sub-cell coverage, and cells are roughly twice as tall as they are wide, so even a circle approximated in glyphs comes out distorted (`View.imageCellAspect(_:)` exists for exactly that). Where a round affordance is wanted TUIkit draws a glyph (`●`, `○`). Shapes as a whole wait on O0 of the refusal review.

Color.Representation.why: The type of Color's transferRepresentation; see that entry.

Color.transferRepresentation.why: Color's Transferable conformance. CoreTransferable is Apple-only, and the terminal's clipboard holds text: TUIkit's copyable/draggable payloads need no Transferable conformance, so there is no representation for a colour to declare (as for Image.transferRepresentation).

ColorMatrix.why: It exists only as the payload of `GraphicsContext.Filter.colorMatrix`, applied per pixel, and with no `GraphicsContext` there is nothing to apply it. A channel transform of a cell's foreground and background is the colour-effect modifiers' ground (`ColorEffectModifiers.swift`).

ColorRenderingMode.why: It selects the colour space a Canvas or an ImageRenderer composites in, linear or non-linear sRGB. TUIkit has neither, and its one blend, `opacity`, is done in encoded sRGB, so the mode would have nothing to select. If `drawingGroup(opaque:colorMode:)` ships (decisions A27), the type comes with it.

ConcentricRectangle.why: It exists to inset a rounded rectangle so nested corner radii stay concentric; TUIkit's corners are single characters with no radius (Sources/TUIkitStyling/Styles/BorderStyle.swift:69-141), so there is no radius to keep concentric.

ContainerRelativeShape.why: It resolves to the enclosing container's shape, so nested corners stay concentric. No container publishes a shape or a radius: a container draws a `BorderStyle` box whose corners are single glyphs, so there is nothing to be concentric with.

ContentShapeKinds.why: The option set naming which shape is being set (interaction / dragPreview / contextMenuPreview / focusEffect). Hit regions are cell rectangles with no shape to specify (Sources/TUIkitCore/Input/HitTestRegion.swift:29-42); the drag-preview kind is served by `.draggable(_:preview:)

ControlSize.why: A point-metrics/type-size class; the terminal owns the font and cell size and every control is one cell-row tall (see the controlSize modifier). There is no scale axis for the enum to select along.

Edge.Corner.why: The corners of a rectangle, with `Edge.Corner.Set` and `Edge.Corner.Style` for the corner radii of `Shape.rect(corners:)` and `RoundedRectangularShapeCorners`. Cells have corners, but every consumer here is a shape, which waits on O0 of the refusal review; the enum would come with them. (The `rawValue`/`allCases` gaps once reported for `Edge` itself were synthesized-conformance false positives: `Edge` is at parity.)

EdgeInsets.init(_:).why: Converts from AppKit/UIKit's NSDirectionalEdgeInsets, whose values are points. TUIkit insets count cells, so the conversion would have to invent a point-to-cell scale; and TUIkit links no AppKit, as it must build on Linux.

EdgeInsets.inset(by:edges:).why: Grows insets by a RectangleCornerInsets, the per-corner radii of a rounded rectangle (declined under its own entry). Cell geometry has no corner radii to add.

Ellipse.why: Same as Circle: curved edges require fractional cell coverage that a glyph cell cannot express, and TUIkit has no path rasterizer — only glyph selection (Sources/TUIkitImage/ShapeSampling.swift is raster-to-glyph matching, not vector drawing).

EmptyMatchedTransitionSourceConfiguratio.why: The empty base value passed into `matchedTransitionSource(id:in:configuration:)`. Inapplicable for the same reason as the protocol it conforms to — no transition machinery, no corner geometry.

EnvironmentValues.allowsTightening.why: The environment half of allowsTightening(_:); absent for the same reason — a cell grid has no inter-character spacing to tighten.

EnvironmentValues.minimumScaleFactor.why: The environment half of minimumScaleFactor(_:); absent for the same reason — glyph size belongs to the terminal emulator, not to the app.

FillShapeView.why: The View produced by Shape.fill(_:); no Shape exists. Filling a rectangular area with a colour is BackgroundModifier (Sources/TUIkit/Modifiers/BackgroundModifier.swift:15-42).

FillStyle.why: eoFill and isAntialiased only mean something to a path rasterizer resolving self-intersection and edge coverage; there is no path and no partial cell coverage (see Shape).

Font.Design.rounded.why: A rounded face. The terminal draws every cell in the one face its user configured, and no escape sequence asks for another. Font.Design ships .default and .monospaced, the two that describe the terminal's face (Documentation/SwiftUI-API-completion-refusal-review.md P1).

Font.Design.serif.why: A serif face. The terminal draws every cell in the one face its user configured, and no escape sequence asks for another; macOS's serif also widens text (31 → 34 pt, measured), which a cell cannot. Font.Design ships .default and .monospaced, the two that describe the terminal's face (Documentation/SwiftUI-API-completion-refusal-review.md P1).

Font.Leading.why: Leading is the space between baselines, measured in fractions of a point. A terminal's baselines are one cell apart, always. The nearest expressible thing is a WHOLE blank row between lines, which TUIkit spells `View.lineSpacing(_:)` (Sources/TUIkit/Modifiers/LineSpacingModifier.swift) — a different unit and a different meaning, so it is not this API under another name.

Font.leading(_:).why: Leading is fractional-point spacing between baselines; a terminal's baselines are exactly one cell apart. The nearest expressible thing is a WHOLE blank row between wrapped lines — `View.lineSpacing(_:)` (Sources/TUIkit/Modifiers/LineSpacingModifier.swift) — a different unit and a different granularity, so it is not this API renamed. See also the `Font.Leading` entry.

Font.Resolved.ctFont.why: A CoreText font, absent on Linux and Windows, and a terminal draws in the one face the user configured: there is no font object to hand out. Font.Resolved ships the flags a cell can vary (refusal review P2).

Font.Resolved.leading.why: Line spacing in points; a terminal's rows are fixed, and TUIkit's lineSpacing counts whole rows. Omitted so the spelling fails to compile.

Font.Resolved.pointSize.why: A terminal draws every cell at one size, the user's, which the app cannot read in points; omitted so the spelling fails to compile rather than answer a guess.

Font.Resolved.width.why: A font's width axis (condensed, expanded) has no cell equivalent: every glyph advances one cell; omitted as Font.Width is.

GeometryEffect.why: Its one requirement, `effectValue(size:) -> ProjectionTransform`, has no representation here (see ProjectionTransform). TUIkit's geometry customisation point is `Layout`, which places children at whole cells.

GeometryProxy.safeAreaInsets.why: Omitted on purpose, as decisions B6 records: TUIkit's chrome is subtracted from what a view is offered before layout, so no content runs under a bar and the insets would always be zero. It becomes real with the fuller safe area B6 prices.

HelpLink.init(anchor:).why: Opens an anchor in an Apple Help book through AppKit's NSHelpManager; a terminal has no Help Viewer and Linux no help books. HelpLink(action:) and HelpLink(destination:) ship. See decisions C5.

HelpLink.init(anchor:book:).why: As HelpLink.init(anchor:): an Apple Help book, through AppKit's NSHelpManager, which a terminal app cannot open. See decisions C5.

Image.init(size:label:opaque:colorMode:r.why: An image drawn by a closure into a GraphicsContext. TUIkit's drawing context is a FrameBuffer (see GraphicsContext under differentShape), and code that draws is a view rather than an image: a Renderable, which draws into the cells it is given at every frame instead of into pixels once.

Image.Representation.why: The type of Image's transferRepresentation; see that entry.

Image.Scale.why: The .small/.medium/.large enum for imageScale; the terminal owns the font size and a symbol is one codepoint at that size (Sources/TUIkit/SFSymbols/SFSymbol.swift:62). Documentation/SwiftUI-compatibility.md:452 records the same constraint for Font generally.

Image.transferRepresentation.why: Image's Transferable conformance. CoreTransferable is Apple-only, and the terminal's clipboard holds text: TUIkit's copyable/draggable payloads need no Transferable conformance, so there is no representation for an image to declare.

ImagePaint.why: A ShapeStyle that fills a shape with a tiled or scaled image, resolved per pixel against the shape's coverage. There are no shapes to fill (O0 of the refusal review), and a raster draws through `Image`, which is TUIkit's raster-to-cell renderer.

InsettableShape.why: It exists so `strokeBorder` can inset a shape by half its line width. A terminal's line is exactly one cell wide and its inset exactly one cell, which `padding` and `border` already express; shapes as a whole wait on O0 of the refusal review.

MatchedGeometryProperties.why: An option set (.position/.size/.frame) selecting which parts of a frame `matchedGeometryEffect` interpolates. With no interpolation to configure — see the matchedGeometryEffect entry, and Documentation/SwiftUI-compatibility.md:452 — the type has nothing to select between.

MatchedTransitionSourceConfiguration.why: Configures a zoom transition's source: its corner shape and background. It waits with `matchedTransitionSource` on O4 of the refusal review (decisions A23).

MaterialActiveAppearance.why: Names the active/inactive/automatic appearance of a Material; there is no Material (no blur, no translucency) and no window-activation state — the terminal emulator owns window focus, and TUIkit's own focus model is per-control (Sources/TUIkit/Focus/FocusManager).

OffsetShape.why: A Shape adapter (Shape.offset(x:y:)); no Shape protocol exists. Whole-cell offsetting of a VIEW does exist as View.offset(x:y:) (Sources/TUIkit/Modifiers/OffsetModifier.swift:71).

OutlineSubgroupChildren.why: The content type of the DisclosureGroup that is SwiftUI's OutlineGroup `Subgroup` parameter, written only inside OutlineGroup's full five-parameter type. TUIkit's OutlineGroup declares the three generic parameters that carry information and drops the two that never vary (`Parent` is always `Leaf`, `Subgroup` always that one DisclosureGroup) — Sources/TUIkit/Views/OutlineGroup.swift — so there is no subgroup for this marker to be the content of. Every initializer, for views and for table rows, is SwiftUI's; only spelling the type out by hand differs. Decisions C10.

Path.why: Bezier control points are fractional; the coordinate space here is integer cells only (CellRect, Sources/TUIkit/Views/GeometryReader.swift:77-95). 0 occurrences of a SwiftUI-like Path under Sources (the three \bPath\b hits are a navigation-path comment and a localisation string).

PreviewContext.why: The canvas-supplied context protocol; no canvas can host a terminal view (see PreviewProvider).

PreviewContextKey.why: Key protocol for PreviewContext, which has no host (see PreviewProvider).

PreviewDevice.why: Names a simulator device for the canvas. A TUIkit app's only "device" is the attached terminal, whose size is read live (`\.terminalWidth`/`\.terminalHeight`, Sources/TUIkit/Environment/ViewEnvironmentKeys.swift:75) and whose glyph repertoire is detected at runtime (TerminalHost)

PreviewModifier.why: Supplies shared context to canvas previews; with no canvas able to host a FrameBuffer-rendering view (see PreviewProvider) there is no preview to modify.

PreviewModifierContent.why: The placeholder content type inside a PreviewModifier; absent for the same canvas-hosting reason.

PreviewPlatform.why: Enumerates iOS/macOS/tvOS/watchOS canvases; TUIkit targets a tty on macOS/Linux (Windows in progress) and has no canvas on any of them.

PreviewProvider.why: Xcode's canvas instantiates a PreviewProvider and hosts the resulting view in a real view hierarchy. A TUIkit view resolves to a text `FrameBuffer`, with no NSView or UIView to host, so the canvas has nothing to show; the headless equivalent is the public `renderOnce(content:)`.

ProjectionTransform.why: A 3×3 matrix over continuous coordinates, produced by GeometryEffect and consumed by `projectionEffect`. TUIkit's geometry is whole cells with no matrix: its only spatial operation is a whole-cell offset. The transforms wait on decisions A27.

RectangleCornerRadii.why: Four CGFloat radii; there is no radius anywhere in TUIkit's chrome model — BorderStyle stores four corner Characters instead (Sources/TUIkitStyling/Styles/BorderStyle.swift:13-22).

RotatedShape.why: A Shape adapter for rotation; neither Shape nor rotation exists on a cell grid (see rotationEffect — glyphs cannot be rotated and wide cells cannot be transposed).

RoundedCornerStyle.why: circular vs continuous (squircle) corner curvature is a difference measured well below one cell; both collapse to the same single character (╭) in BorderStyle.rounded (Sources/TUIkitStyling/Styles/BorderStyle.swift:109).

RoundedRectangle.why: A corner radius needs sub-cell coverage to round; the terminal's rounded corner is a single character — BorderStyle.rounded uses ╭╮╰╯ (Sources/TUIkitStyling/Styles/BorderStyle.swift:109-128) — with exactly one radius, take it or leave it.

RoundedRectangularShape.why: A protocol abstracting over rounded-rectangle shapes and their corner treatment; TUIkit has no shapes and no corner radii — a container outline is BorderStyle's eight fixed characters (Sources/TUIkitStyling/Styles/BorderStyle.swift:13-34).

RoundedRectangularShapeCorners.why: Names which corners of a rounded rectangle are rounded; a terminal corner is one character that either IS the rounded glyph (╭) or is not (Sources/TUIkitStyling/Styles/BorderStyle.swift:69-128) — there is no partial-corner state to describe.

SafeAreaRegions.why: An option set over `.container` and `.keyboard`. Neither is a live distinction here: a terminal has no on-screen keyboard, and the container region is the whole grid less the chrome the app declared, subtracted before layout (decisions B6).

ScaledShape.why: A Shape adapter for scaling; neither Shape nor sub-cell scaling exists (glyph size is the terminal's font, see scaleEffect).

ScrollEdgeEffectStyle.why: It selects a hard or soft fade of scrolled content passing beneath a bar. No content passes beneath chrome here, the bars being subtracted from what a view is offered (decisions B6), so today it would draw nothing; it waits on O7 of the refusal review.

ScrollInputKind.why: Its values are watchOS's — the Digital Crown and the double-tap hand-gesture shortcut — and the macOS SDK defines none, so no macOS source can name one, and View.scrollInputBehavior(_:for:) cannot be called there either. A terminal has neither input. The question macOS code can ask, whether scrolling is allowed at all, is .scrollDisabled (the ScrollInputBehavior entry).

ScrollView.showsIndicators.why: The stored property behind the soft-deprecated ScrollView(_:showsIndicators:content:) initializer, which TUIkit omits as it omits every soft-deprecated spelling; .scrollIndicators(_:axes:) is the current one. The property alone would give that modifier a second, hidden answer, the confusion ScrollView.init's comment records splitting visibility from style was meant to end. Decisions-W10 C-W10-2 prices adding it.

SectionedFetchRequest.why: A Core Data property wrapper (its partner `\.managedObjectContext` is absent too). Core Data exists on no platform TUIkit builds for besides Apple's, and the repository's rules require macOS and Linux, with Windows in progress, so it cannot be a dependency. Decisions A18 covers Apple-only API behind `canImport`.

SectionedFetchResults.why: The results collection of SectionedFetchRequest; same Core Data dependency, excluded by the cross-platform requirement in .claude/CLAUDE.md (Linux and Windows builds have no CoreData).

ShadowStyle.why: It parameterises drop/inner shadows by radius and fractional offset, both sub-cell quantities on a grid whose smallest unit is one whole cell (CellRect is Int-only, Sources/TUIkit/Views/GeometryReader.swift:77-95). See `shadow`.

Shape.why: A Shape is `path(in:) -> Path` over continuous coordinates, rasterised with antialiasing, and a cell has no partial coverage. TUIkit draws its one shape, the rectangle, from box-drawing characters through `BorderStyle`. Shapes as a whole wait on O0 of the refusal review, which fixes their unit.

ShapeRole.why: It tells a ShapeStyle whether it is filling, stroking, or drawing a separator, so the style can adapt; there is no Shape and no ShapeStyle. The separator role does have a colour home — Palette.border, which Divider defaults to (Sources/TUIkit/Views/Spacer.swift:138).

ShapeView.why: The protocol that makes a filled/stroked Shape a View; with no Shape and no fill/stroke rasterization there is nothing to conform. TUIkit's equivalent leaf-drawing hook is Renderable (Sources/TUIkitView/Rendering/Renderable.swift:53).

StrokeBorderShapeView.why: The View produced by InsettableShape.strokeBorder; its whole reason for existing is insetting by half a fractional line width, which cannot arise when the line is one indivisible cell.

StrokeShapeView.why: The View produced by Shape.stroke(_:style:); with no Shape and a fixed one-cell stroke there is nothing to construct. Rectangle stroking is View.border(...) (Sources/TUIkit/Extensions/View+Layout.swift:36).

StrokeStyle.why: Line width, dash, cap, join and miter limit are all sub-cell quantities. A terminal stroke is one cell wide and its style is which character repeats: `BorderStyle`'s line, double line, heavy and rounded, the closest thing TUIkit has. Shapes wait on O0 of the refusal review.

SubmitLabel.why:
It names an on-screen keyboard's Return key ('Go', 'Send', 'Search'), and a terminal has no on-screen keyboard. It shipped once as a value stored in the environment that nothing read, which is worse than absence — the call compiled and the developer never learned the affordance does not exist — so it was removed (c5f31f85) and `.submitLabel(.send)` now fails to compile. `.onSubmit`, the behaviour rather than the legend, is fully implemented.

The obvious substitute WAS evaluated and declined 2026-08-17: a status-bar hint ('⏎ Send') while the field holds focus, using the per-focus-section registration StatusBarState already has. Four reasons. (1) It would fight the app for the Return slot: a StatusBarItem's identity IS its shortcut (StatusBarItem.swift — the hover state machine compares it across renders) and `resolvedSectionItems` drops any global item sharing one, so focusing a field would evict an app's own '⏎ select' item and restore it on blur. (2) It could lie: Return only submits when a submit action exists — `combinedSubmitAction` returns nil otherwise, deliberately, so Return falls through to a dialog's default button — so a field with `.submitLabel(.send)` and no `.onSubmit` would advertise 'Send' while Return fired 'Cancel'. Suppressing the hint in that case diverges from SwiftUI, which shows the label regardless. (3) Chrome churn: items joining and leaving on every Tab shift the bar, and at narrow widths can flip it into renderCompact, changing the other items too. (4) `\.statusBar` is Optional, so it would be inert in an app that does not use the bar — the honesty guarantee would not be unconditional.

If revisited, the shape to build is opt-in app/scene-level chrome (a TUI-specific `.submitLabelHint(_:)`, default off) so `.submitLabel` is data the app chooses to render, the Return slot is only contended when asked for, and (2) becomes the app's explicit choice. Trigger to reconsider: a real app wanting it.

SymbolColorRenderingMode.why: gradient vs flat colouring inside one symbol needs sub-glyph colour addressing; the smallest colourable unit is the whole cell (one SGR foreground per run — Sources/TUIkit/Rendering/ANSIRenderer.swift).

SymbolEffectTransition.why: A Transition that plays a symbol's appear, disappear or replace effect, built from the Symbols framework's effect types (TransitionSymbolEffect, SymbolEffectOptions), which do not exist on Linux or Windows. Whether TUIkit declares its own Symbols vocabulary for the effects one glyph can show is A35 of Documentation/SwiftUI-API-completion-decisions-W12.md (and A18); TUIkit's Transition protocol itself ships.

SymbolRenderingMode.why: Names monochrome, hierarchical, palette and multicolour symbol rendering. Only monochrome survives a cell grid: a symbol is one code point drawn in the cell's single foreground colour, so a type distinguishing four modes would have exactly one that changes anything.

SymbolVariableValueMode.why: How a variable-value symbol shows its fraction, by colour or by drawing, both defined over the symbol's layers. TUIkit draws a symbol as one glyph with no layers; the terminal's way of showing a fraction is a glyph ramp, which `ProgressView`, `Gauge` and `Slider` draw.

TabBarMinimizeBehavior.why: Exists only to feed `tabBarMinimizeBehavior(_:)`; the minimized state is a translucent floating pill at a fraction of the bar's height, which a grid of opaque whole-row cells cannot represent.

Text.Layout.why: Lines, runs and run slices with typographic bounds, handed to a `TextRenderer`. TUIkit's laid-out text is a `FrameBuffer` of styled strings with whole-cell widths: no glyphs, no baselines and no fractional positions. It waits with `TextRenderer` on O16 of the refusal review.

Text.LayoutKey.why: The preference key that publishes anchored Text.Layout values (glyph geometry in a coordinate space) to ancestors. Depends entirely on the glyph-layout model TUIkit does not and cannot have — the app emits characters and the emulator does the typesetting.

TextAttribute.why: Marker protocol for values attached via Text.customAttribute and read back inside a TextRenderer's glyph-run walk. It exists only to feed the custom-rendering pipeline, which has no terminal counterpart (no glyph runs, no drawing context).

TextInputFormattingControlPlacement.why: Names the OS surfaces (the keyboard's accessory bar, an inspector, a menu) where the system's rich-text formatting controls appear, for `textInputFormattingControlVisibility`. A terminal app has no OS-drawn chrome on its fields: every cell on screen is written by the process itself.

TextProxy.why: The handle a TextRenderer uses to resolve a Text into a Text.Layout of glyph runs with typographic bounds. Same reason as TextRenderer — TUIkit never materialises glyphs; it emits characters and lets the terminal rasterize.

TextRenderer.why: Protocol whose draw(layout:in:) receives glyph runs and a GraphicsContext. TUIkit's rendering primitive is FrameBuffer (styled strings + integer cell widths); there is no rasterizer in-process, so there is no glyph, no outline, and no context to draw into.

ToolbarTitleDisplayMode.why: Exists only to feed `toolbarTitleDisplayMode(_:)`; a cell grid has a single glyph size (TUIkit has no Font type), so `.large`/`.inline`/`.inlineLarge` collapse to one representation.

TransformedShape.why: A Shape adapter carrying a CGAffineTransform; the grid supports only integer translation (View.offset, Sources/TUIkit/Modifiers/OffsetModifier.swift:71) and there is no Shape to transform.

UnevenRoundedRectangle.why: Per-corner radii presuppose a radius at all; BorderStyle names four corner CHARACTERS (topLeft/topRight/bottomLeft/bottomRight, Sources/TUIkitStyling/Styles/BorderStyle.swift:13-22), which is the terminal's whole corner vocabulary.

View.allowsTightening(_:).why: It asks the type setter to reduce inter-character spacing so a line fits without truncating. A TUIkit app emits characters and the emulator advances a whole cell per column — 1 for most, 2 for East Asian wide and most emoji, 0 for combining marks. There is no sub-cell spacing to reduce. Fitting text into less space is spelled truncationMode(_:), lineLimit(_:) or ViewThatFits here.

View.minimumScaleFactor(_:).why: It permits shrinking the FONT to fit, down to a fraction of the nominal size. A TUIkit app does not own the font: cell size belongs to the emulator, is chosen by the user, and is identical for every glyph on screen. Nothing in the framework can scale one view's text without scaling the whole terminal.

View.scrollInputBehavior(_:for:).why: Takes a ScrollInputKind, which has no value on macOS (see that entry), so no macOS source can call it.

View.submitLabel(_:).why:
It names an on-screen keyboard's Return key ('Go', 'Send', 'Search'), and a terminal has no on-screen keyboard. It shipped once as a value stored in the environment that nothing read, which is worse than absence — the call compiled and the developer never learned the affordance does not exist — so it was removed (c5f31f85) and `.submitLabel(.send)` now fails to compile. `.onSubmit`, the behaviour rather than the legend, is fully implemented.

The obvious substitute WAS evaluated and declined 2026-08-17: a status-bar hint ('⏎ Send') while the field holds focus, using the per-focus-section registration StatusBarState already has. Four reasons. (1) It would fight the app for the Return slot: a StatusBarItem's identity IS its shortcut (StatusBarItem.swift — the hover state machine compares it across renders) and `resolvedSectionItems` drops any global item sharing one, so focusing a field would evict an app's own '⏎ select' item and restore it on blur. (2) It could lie: Return only submits when a submit action exists — `combinedSubmitAction` returns nil otherwise, deliberately, so Return falls through to a dialog's default button — so a field with `.submitLabel(.send)` and no `.onSubmit` would advertise 'Send' while Return fired 'Cancel'. Suppressing the hint in that case diverges from SwiftUI, which shows the label regardless. (3) Chrome churn: items joining and leaving on every Tab shift the bar, and at narrow widths can flip it into renderCompact, changing the other items too. (4) `\.statusBar` is Optional, so it would be inert in an app that does not use the bar — the honesty guarantee would not be unconditional.

If revisited, the shape to build is opt-in app/scene-level chrome (a TUI-specific `.submitLabelHint(_:)`, default off) so `.submitLabel` is data the app chooses to render, the Return slot is only contended when asked for, and (2) becomes the app's explicit choice. Trigger to reconsider: a real app wanting it.

WindowManagerRole.why: It tells the macOS window manager how to place/associate a window. A TUIkit app has exactly one surface — the terminal's alternate screen buffer — and no window manager to negotiate with; `WindowGroup` exists purely as the scene-shaped entry point (Sources/TUIkit/App/Scene.swift)

WindowToolbarFullScreenVisibility.why: Exists only to feed `windowToolbarFullScreenVisibility(_:)`; TUIkit has no window and no window toolbar — the host terminal owns both, and TUIkit only ever knows a rows×columns grid (Sources/TUIkit/App/RenderLoop.swift).

ToolbarDefaultItemKind.title.why: Removes the default title item SwiftUI puts in a window's toolbar. TUIkit draws no default title to remove: there is no toolbar, the terminal owns the window title, and the in-grid `.appHeader` is content the app writes itself. `ToolbarDefaultItemKind.sidebarToggle` is implemented (Sources/TUIkit/Modifiers/ToolbarRemovalModifier.swift).

ToolbarDefaultItemKind.search.why: Removes the search field SwiftUI places in a window's toolbar by default. TUIkit has no toolbar for a search item to sit in: `.searchable` draws its field at the top of the searchable subtree, where the app put the modifier (Sources/TUIkit/Extensions/View+Searchable.swift), so there is no framework-placed item to take away. `ToolbarDefaultItemKind.sidebarToggle` is implemented (Sources/TUIkit/Modifiers/ToolbarRemovalModifier.swift).

KeyEquivalent.clear.why: The keypad Clear key (U+F739). No terminal encoding TUIkit parses gives it a sequence of its own (it sits in Num Lock's position), so a shortcut or onKeyPress on it could never fire. Reopen if a terminal is found to send it, most likely under the kitty keyboard protocol (decisions A4). See decisions C4.

DebugReplaceableView.why: Xcode's previews machinery: the type Xcode substitutes for a view while it hot-reloads a preview. It exists for the Xcode preview canvas, which never hosts a TUIkit view.

AccessibilityActionKind.how: KeyboardShortcut.defaultAction / .cancelAction, the context-menu keyboard route, onDelete
AccessibilityActionKind.why: Its cases are the standard actions, and each has a real key binding in TUIkit: `.default` is the default action (Return activates the default button), `.escape` the cancel action, `.showMenu` the context-menu keyboard route, and `.delete` a row's `onDelete`.

AccessibilityFocusState.why: SwiftUI needs a second focus-state wrapper because VoiceOver's cursor moves independently of keyboard focus. A terminal has one focus, which `@FocusState` with `focused(_:)` and `focused(_:equals:)` binds (`Sources/TUIkit/Focus/FocusState.swift`).

Anchor.why: The general `Anchor<Value>` is absent; it waits with the anchor preferences on decisions A2. Its one consumer that shipped, a popover's attachment anchor, takes `PopoverAttachmentAnchor`: `.rect(.bounds)` or `.point(_:)`.

Canvas.why: The immediate-mode drawing surface is a conformance: `Renderable`'s `renderToBuffer(context:) -> FrameBuffer`, with FrameBuffer's public initialisers to build the cells. A SwiftUI-shaped `Canvas` over a `GraphicsContext` waits on shapes (O0 of the refusal review), as the review's D3 note says.

DefaultPickerStyle.why: Sources/TUIkit/Styles/PickerStyle.swift — `.automatic` ships alongside `.inline`, `.menu` and the TUI-specific `.radioGroup`.

DefaultToolbarItem.why: /Users/robot/Documents/TUIkit/Sources/TUIkit/StatusBar/SystemStatusBarItem.swift:22,35,48 — the concrete system-provided items, plus `SystemStatusBarItem.items(onQuit:onAppearance:onTheme:)` at :73 for re-binding their actions.

DynamicViewContent.why: `DynamicViewContentActions` (`Sources/TUIkit/Views/DynamicViewContent.swift`) is the internal seam behind SwiftUI's protocol, whose `onMove` and `onDelete` it mirrors. It behaves the same for ForEach; the cost of its being internal is that a custom row container cannot take part.

EditableCollectionContent.why: The same internal seam, `DynamicViewContentActions` (move, delete and drop-insertion actions an enclosing List discovers), with ForEach conforming. The public surface is ForEach's own `onDelete` and `onMove` rather than a protocol.

EnvironmentObject.why: `@Environment(M.self)` with `.environment(_:)` for an `Observable` object; `Environment` itself is the shared type. A deliberate choice in the compatibility doc's §2.3: Observation only, no `ObservableObject`.

EveryMinuteTimelineSchedule.Entries.next.how: `EveryMinuteTimelineSchedule.Entries` is a typealias for `PeriodicTimelineSchedule.Entries`, whose `next()` it is
EveryMinuteTimelineSchedule.Entries.next.why: The two schedules yield the same kind of sequence, evenly spaced dates, so TUIkit's EveryMinuteTimelineSchedule.Entries is a typealias for PeriodicTimelineSchedule.Entries where SwiftUI nests a type of its own. The member exists; the symbol graph files it under the alias's target, so the tool cannot see it under this path.

FocusedObject.why: SwiftUI's @FocusedObject reads an ObservableObject, the Combine-based family TUIkit does not support (Documentation/SwiftUI-compatibility.md §2.3). The same reading of an @Observable model is `@FocusedValue(Model.self)` (Sources/TUIkit/Focus/FocusedValue.swift), which SwiftUI also offers and which tracks the properties the body reads, as the ObservableObject wrapper did through objectWillChange.

ForEach.Body.why: ForEach declares `public var body: Never`, as SwiftUI's non-tab ForEach does. The `Body` typealias is inferred rather than written, so symbolgraph-extract emits it for the SDK's interface and not for TUIkit's source: an extraction artifact, not a gap.

GestureState.why: The transient per-gesture state a drag needs is held by `DragGestureModifier` and handed to the closure with its start position and phase (`DragGestureEvent.Phase`: began, moved, ended), so no property wrapper is needed to keep it.

GraphicsContext.why: `FrameBuffer` is the drawing context: `composited(with:at:)` to draw, `replacingLines` to write, `clamped(toWidth:height:)` to clip, and its overlays, hit-test regions and animated cells as the layer, interaction and animation channels. It differs in drawing cells, not paths; a path-drawing context waits on O0 of the refusal review.

List.Body.why: Sources/TUIkit/Views/List.swift:96 `public var body: some View`, the same shape as SwiftUI's `typealias Body = some View`. The typealias is inferred in TUIkit's source and written in the SDK interface, so the gap is a symbolgraph artifact.

Material.why: The scrim role a material plays for modals exists: `View.dimmed()` recolours what is behind a modal toward the palette, and `Palette.overlayBackground` paints an overlay's surface. A material as a translucent palette surface is O5 of the refusal review.

ObservedObject.how: a plain @Observable reference, or @Bindable for write-through
ObservedObject.why: `@Bindable` (shipped) for write-through, or a plain `@Observable` reference passed in, with Observation doing the invalidation. The compatibility doc's §2.3 maps `@ObservedObject var m: M` to those.

ScrollInputBehavior.why: Sources/TUIkit/Views/ScrollDisabled.swift:66. SwiftUI's automatic/enabled/disabled triple collapses to the Bool environment value; the non-additive nesting semantics match (ScrollDisabled.swift:60-63).

ScrollView.Body.why: Sources/TUIkit/Views/ScrollView.swift:118 `public var body: some View`. axes and content are public (:79, :82), so Body is the only listed gap and it is an inferred-typealias extraction artifact.

ScrollViewReader.Body.why: Sources/TUIkit/Views/ScrollViewReader.swift:83 `public var body: some View`; same inferred-typealias artifact.

SearchUnavailableContent.why: /Users/robot/Documents/TUIkit/Sources/TUIkit/Views/ContentUnavailableView.swift:126 and :140 — the same two entry points SwiftUI exposes through SearchUnavailableContent, spelled as statics on the shared ContentUnavailableView type.

Section.Body.why: TUIkit's Section has a real `body: some View` returning `_SectionCore`, per the project's rule that a public control is a View with a real body. SwiftUI's declares `Body = Never` and renders as a primitive, so the differing typealias is a deliberate structural choice.

Spacer.minLength.why: `Spacer.minLength` is internal while `init(minLength:)` is public, so the value can be set but not read back under SwiftUI's name. The public read-back is `spacerMinLength`, from the TUI-specific `SpacerProtocol`.

StateObject.why: Documentation/SwiftUI-compatibility.md:179 states the mapping explicitly; `State` is a shared type (Sources/TUIkitView/State/State.swift) and binds at render time by the view's own identity.

TapGesture.why: /Users/robot/Documents/TUIkit/Sources/TUIkit/Extensions/View+Events.swift:135 and :169; the count form uses the dispatcher's synthesised `MouseEvent.clickCount` (terminals report no double-click, so it is timed). The located form hands the tap a `CellPoint`, not a CGPoint (§2.2).

Text.Body.why: Extraction artifact, not a real gap: TUIkit's Text declares `public var body: Never`, so `Body` is inferred as `Never` exactly as in SwiftUI. An inferred typealias is absent from the symbol graph of source, as `ForEach.Body` is.

ToolbarItemPlacement.why: `StatusBarItemOrder` (a sort key, lower first) and `StatusBarAlignment` (leading, trailing, centre, justified). Position within the one bar is a sort key plus a bar-wide alignment, not a semantic placement; toolbars are decisions A28.

ToolbarPlacement.how: choice of modifier: .appHeader (top surface) vs .statusBarItems (bottom surface)
ToolbarPlacement.why: The choice of modifier: `.appHeader` for the top surface, `.statusBarItems` for the bottom. Both surfaces are real and drawn outside the view tree, their rows subtracted from what the content is offered; toolbars are decisions A28.

View.fixedSize().how: View.fixedSize(horizontal:vertical:) — both parameters default to true
View.fixedSize().why: SwiftUI declares two overloads; TUIkit's single one has defaults, so `.fixedSize()` compiles and means the same thing (verified by a `swiftc -typecheck` probe against the built module, not by reading). Adding a no-argument overload would be a second spelling of one idea — what the consolidate-before-adding rule exists to prevent — and the extractor cannot see that a defaulted parameter list already covers the shorter call, so it reports the shape difference as a gap.

View.focusedObject(_:).why: Publishes an ObservableObject (§2.3: no Combine-based family). `.focusedValue(_ object:)` publishes an @Observable object under its type, read back with `@FocusedValue(Model.self)` (Sources/TUIkit/Modifiers/FocusedValueModifier.swift).

View.focusedSceneObject(_:).why: Publishes an ObservableObject for the scene (§2.3: no Combine-based family). `.focusedSceneValue(_ object:)` publishes an @Observable object under its type, seen wherever the focus is (Sources/TUIkit/Modifiers/FocusedValueModifier.swift).
